title: the Arthashastra's opening
tomorrow: a book famous for one thing has a chapter on another. which?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Arthashastra's opening balanced three aims and called artha chief, the floor the others stand on. Today, the last of this run, and an argument it holds inside one chapter.

Any school handbook starts the fight on its own. Should seniors get different rules from freshmen? Captains different from the bench? Or one rulebook for everybody? The Arthashastra's chapter on the Vedas holds both answers at once, and readers have leaned on each side of it.
screen: `DIFFERENT RULES FOR DIFFERENT JOBS?` → `OR ONE RULEBOOK FOR ALL?` → `ONE CHAPTER HOLDS BOTH.`

segments.voice: Most of the chapter sets out svadharma, each person's own duty, by station and stage of life: the student's, the householder's, the ruler's, and duties tied to birth. It says that keeping one's own duty leads to heaven and endless joy, and that when duties are mixed up, the world falls into confusion. Hear that view at its strongest. Roles really do differ. A judge owes things a farmer doesn't, and a parent owes things a child doesn't. A community holds together when each person does their own part well. Then, in a single line, the chapter names duties common to all: not harming, truthfulness, purity, freedom from spite, freedom from cruelty, and forgiveness. Hear that view at its strongest too. Whatever your station, this list doesn't change. It's the floor under every role, and it doesn't care who your parents were. Some readers through the centuries put the weight on the stations. Some modern Hindu readers put the shared list first, especially where station meant rank by birth, the ranking Ambedkar refused. Both readings start from the same page. That's where this run on the Arthashastra's opening ends: duties that differ, and a short list that doesn't.
screen: `SVADHARMA: YOUR OWN DUTY.` · `ROLES DIFFER, AND THAT HOLDS US UP.` · `A SHORT LIST FOR EVERYONE.` · `READERS LEAN BOTH WAYS.` · then, large: `DUTIES THAT DIFFER, A FLOOR THAT DOESN'T.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes if that's comfortable. On each slow breath, bring to mind one role you hold, child, friend, student, worker, and one duty that comes with it. For the last few breaths, let the roles fall away, and rest on what you'd owe anyone at all: the truth, and no cruelty.
The Arthashastra's opening: each person's own duty, and under every station a short list for all, from not harming to forgiveness.
Keep this: the Arthashastra's opening, own duties above and a shared floor beneath. That's the end of this run.

howItsDone: Hindu teachers often distinguish svadharma, the duties of one's own station and stage of life, from duties common to everyone; the Arthashastra's chapter on the Vedas is one early place where both are named.
